chapters.title: Thingness, establishment, and the nonexistent
chapters.question: Does an intelligible object require extramental existence to be a thing?
chapters.evidence: Ṭūsī equates the extension of thingness with existence and rejects external establishment of a possible quiddity without existence. Iṣfahānī distinguishes the Muʿtazilī claim about an uninstantiated possible quiddity from an impossible object; the controversy is not whether one may think about the nonexistent. The later Akbarī fixed entities must be examined independently, not used as a retroactive translation of Muʿtazilī thubūt.
chapters.AT: Aertsen distinguishes res, understood in relation to quiddity, from ens, understood through being. Test whether a common linguistic or conceptual subject permits an ontological commitment; do not infer a separate entity merely from successful predication.
chapters.open: The exact status of a possible-but-nonexistent object, and of a fixed entity known by God, remains an inter-tradition disagreement. Later authors can reject extramental thubūt yet retain objective truth about unrealized possibilities.
chapters.comparison: Compare the quantifiers in the controversy: a possible quiddity can be conceived without having extramental being. Iṣfahānī and al-Ḥillī dispute the move from conceptual determinacy to an external “thing”; Jurjānī demands that the opposing meanings of thubūt be kept distinct. Al-Taftāzānī offers a separate Sunni denial of a third ontic state. None of these positions yet settles the Akbarī aʿyān thābita doctrine, which is not simply the old Muʿtazilī proposition in later vocabulary.

chapters.title: Existence, essence, participation, and actuality
chapters.question: Is existence other than quiddity, and what makes the existing individual actual?
chapters.evidence: Qūnawī challenges the supposed identity of the Necessary Existent’s reality and existence using a trilemma based on the common concept of existence. Ṭūsī replies by distinguishing uniform predication from differentiated or graded predication. Later commentators debate mental versus extramental addition. Ṭihrānī’s section on quiddity considered in itself is essential because the naked quiddity must not be assumed to subsist independently.
chapters.AT: Compare Aertsen’s subjectum–essentia–esse with Avicennian māhiyya–wujūd. The recognition that existence is intellectually additional to quiddity is not yet proof of Aquinas’s actus essendi or a real composition of two elements.
chapters.open: A full integration must demonstrate what actus essendi explains that conceptual addition does not, and whether this requires substantial or formal mediation. Avoid identifying wujūd, thubūt, and esse by vocabulary alone.
chapters.comparison: Qūnawī argues from one common concept of existence to a dilemma about God’s reality. Ṭūsī does not deny conceptual commonality; he denies that the concept must apply uniformly to all its instances. Al-Taftāzānī’s clarification of “addition” strengthens the need to distinguish conceptual otherness from extramental composition. The Thomistic comparison must establish why esse has a distinct explanatory function; shared vocabulary does not establish that doctrine.

chapters.title: Mental existence and the object known
chapters.question: When we know heat or humanity, what exists in the mind?
chapters.evidence: The mental-existence selections distinguish the reality represented, its form in the intellect, and the accidental cognitive occurrence. Iṣfahānī, Jurjānī, Qūshjī, and Lāhījī cannot be collapsed into one thesis. Ṭihrānī explicitly deploys logical statements about real propositions to defend mental existence and asks why thinking heat does not heat the mind.
chapters.AT: Aquinas’s intelligible species and the identity of knower and known under an intentional aspect supply a parallel, not an identity. Whether the mental object falls under the same category as its extramental instance is a decisive test of the theory.
chapters.open: Distinguish knowledge by presence, ordinary mental existence, and spiritual witnessing; none should be assimilated merely because all involve a presence to consciousness.
chapters.comparison: Al-Ḥillī and al-Lāhījī examine how mental representation can be of heat without producing heat in the knowing subject. Al-Taftāzānī explicitly distinguishes an intellectual form from the thing’s effect-bearing concrete identity. Al-Qūshjī’s discussion of cognitive qualities gives a further angle. The dispute is not merely whether we can think of nonexistent objects, but what actually obtains in an act of knowing.

chapters.title: Nafs al-amr, objective truth, and divine exemplarity
chapters.question: How can a proposition be objectively true without a currently existing material instance?
chapters.evidence: Ṭihrānī distinguishes what a thing is in itself from its consideration by a knower. His explanation of a real proposition requires correspondence to a determinate objective situation and not simply a matching concept in another human mind. In the Akbarī material, the distinction between the Real and finite intellectual determinations raises a different problem concerning adequacy of metaphysical predication.
chapters.AT: Aertsen argues for the thing as measure of human knowledge and God’s intellect as exemplary measure of the thing. Compare these two measures with nafs al-amr without collapsing a truth condition into a theological ground of existence.
chapters.open: A particularly difficult case is the truth of a proposition about impossible, absent, or future entities: specify whether the ground is the quiddity, a conditional, divine knowledge, or an independent status.
chapters.comparison: Ṭihrānī supplies a direct discussion of correspondence and nafs al-amr. Al-Jurjānī’s Sunni argument shows how a *concept* of the nonexistent can be distinct without requiring an extramentally established nonexistent entity. Keep the truth of a proposition distinct from an ontic theory about the subject of the proposition. Later divine-exemplar accounts need a separate argument and cannot be smuggled into a theory of correspondence.

chapters.title: Necessity, possibility, origination, and dependence
chapters.question: Why does a possible being need a cause, even after it begins to exist?
chapters.evidence: Ḥillī argues that possibility rather than origination grounds causal dependence: origination is posterior to being brought about, while the need for a cause precedes the act of production in explanatory order. Rāzī’s selected parallel holds that the persistent possible remains dependent. This argument has a precise target: a causal theory based entirely on temporal origination.
chapters.AT: Aertsen distinguishes the necessity internal to a nature from creaturely dependence. A being may be naturally incorruptible while remaining caused; wujūb bi-ghayrihi does not imply wujūb bi-dhātihi.
chapters.open: Keep wujūb, modal ḍarūra, and epistemic ʿilm ḍarūrī distinct; proof of causal dependence is not proof of Thomistic creation or concurrence without a further argument.
chapters.comparison: Al-Ḥillī’s argument that origination is explanatorily posterior to existence must be read beside Rāzī’s insistence that the persisting possible remains dependent. Al-Taftāzānī’s critique of an inference requiring new conditions questions a necessitarian premise, rather than simply denying that possible beings require causes. These authors are addressing different moments in the explanatory order.

chapters.title: Demonstration, definition, and scientific questioning
chapters.question: What transforms a sound inference into an explanatory demonstration?
chapters.evidence: The comparison must proceed beyond the Tajrīd to Avicenna’s Burhān and the post-Avicennian logic tradition. Distinguish knowing whether something is, knowing what it is, and knowing why a predicate belongs to it. Ṭihrānī’s later criticism of the alleged pure demonstrative form of the ṣiddīqīn proof is identified, but the passage itself still requires a fresh checked translation.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s reconstruction of Aquinas derives philosophical questioning from the search for a middle term that is not merely syllogistic but causal. Compare the status of essential definitions, middle terms, and an explanatory proof.
chapters.open: Do not convert “Qutb criticized Aristotelian definitions” into “Qutb rejected all rational demonstration.” Suhrawardī’s critique in the Ishrāq materials attacks the sufficiency of the Peripatetic differentia and definition apparatus.
chapters.comparison: Aertsen’s AT concern about explanation has a particularly fruitful Islamic counterpart in the distinction between conception and assent. The Sunni logical dispute involves whether definitions provide essences and whether proofs reveal causes. Ibn Taymiyya reports the logicians’ standard division in the course of a detailed criticism. Shīrāzī explains the middle term as the inferential connector; that alone does not show that the middle is an intrinsic causal explanation.

chapters.title: Predication, categories, second intelligibles, and reality
chapters.question: Which logical divisions disclose real divisions, and which are only intellectual considerations?
chapters.evidence: The commentary debate depends on whether shared predication of existence implies one extramental property, how a universal is conceived, and what constitutes a second intelligible. Ṭūsī’s reply to Qūnawī explicitly distinguishes a univocal common concept from gradated instances. Ṭihrānī’s discussion of relations and their correlates supplies a later critical example.
chapters.AT: Compare Aertsen’s two tracks of predication, per se and per participationem. An ontological reconstruction must not infer extramental composition from the surface grammar of “X is Y.”
chapters.open: The test case is whether existence is an accident in the same sense as whiteness, and whether the response requires a theory of analogical predication and real act.
chapters.comparison: This chapter is where the role of logical second intentions must be controlled most tightly. Al-Ḥillī classifies thingness as a second intelligible; al-Taftāzānī accepts a common concept of existence even in authors denying mental existence. Shīrāzī limits substance–accident classification to existing possible beings, not the Necessary Existent. The metaphysical burden is to justify when a distinction in predication requires corresponding distinct principles in reality.

chapters.title: Substantial unity, corporeal constitution, and formal cause
chapters.question: What makes a body or living thing one natural substance rather than an arrangement?
chapters.evidence: The post-classical record maintains at least three rival physical ontologies: atomism, matter–form composition, and Illuminationist extension-based accounts. A label “material cause” in a glossary does not establish acceptance of prime matter. Qutb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī’s Sharḥ Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq devotes a major critical locus to rejection of Peripatetic prime matter and form (printed around p.230).
chapters.AT: For Aquinas, an intrinsic form makes a thing specifically actual and grounds its characteristic operations; the act of being is a further metaphysical actuality. These need independent demonstration.
chapters.open: This topic is a priority for retrieval because the success of the integration of faculties, habits, and natural ends depends on a defensible account of substantial unity.
chapters.comparison: A classification of material and formal causes does not prove hylomorphism. The *Tajrīd* debates must therefore be confronted with the later Sunni accounts of body and with Shīrāzī’s sustained discussion of Suhrawardī’s rejection of Peripatetic matter and form. The presently extracted Shīrāzī text establishes categorial boundaries but not his detailed solution on this issue; the printed sections at pp. 230–244 and 261–264 must be collated before a doctrinal judgment.

chapters.title: Potentiality, actuality, change, and motion
chapters.question: Does motion presuppose a persisting subject actualized through intrinsic principles?
chapters.evidence: Ṭihrānī separates motion as an externally real condition of being-in-transit from the extended traversal assembled in imagination. The distinction interacts with the ontology of relations and with potentiality and actuality. No conclusion about modern physical motion follows merely from this classical analysis.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s natural order treats movement through matter and form; the creative order treats esse as the actuality of all acts. These are not the same application of act/potency.
chapters.open: Explicitly distinguish quwwa as potency, faculty, or capacity from qudra as an agent’s power; connect the two orders only with a warranted account of actualization.
chapters.comparison: Ṭihrānī distinguishes motion understood as being between limits from the extended, mentally constructed traverse; this matters for the ontological status of motion, time, and imaginary succession. Al-Ḥillī’s account of causal ends can illuminate the relation of activity to completion, but does not substitute for a direct comparison of potentiality, actuality, and substantial change.

chapters.title: Four causes, complete causes, instruments, and conditions
chapters.question: Does the four-cause classification exhaust every source of explanation?
chapters.evidence: The existing translations distinguish matter, form, agent, and end, and include questions about instruments, preparations, conditions, and obstacles. Jurjānī distinguishes causes internal to the quiddity from causes of its external existence. Qūshjī presses the completeness of the classification. These distinct causal roles must not be reduced to four sequential efficient causes.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s discussion differentiates the four causes in natural generation, then derives another mode of causing through which being itself is given. The classification of natural causes alone cannot establish divine efficient causality.
chapters.open: The strongest potential reconciliation separates categorical natural causality from transcendental dependence, while testing whether each explanatory term retains content across the transition.
chapters.comparison: Iṣfahānī and Jurjānī differentiate causes of quiddity and causes of existence; al-Ḥillī explicates the final cause’s order of explanation. Qūshjī challenges the exhaustiveness of the classification once conditions and removals of impediments enter. In the Sunni *Mawāqif* tradition, finality and completed causes appear in an extended debate about whether all dependence can be assigned to four headings. The comparison must not assume one simple definition of a “cause”.

chapters.title: Real natural powers and substantial generation
chapters.question: Do created agents really produce their characteristic effects, including new substances?
chapters.evidence: The historical question is broader than whether fire heats. A philosopher may affirm real preparatory influence but attribute substantial forms to a separate giver. The post-Tajrīd authors’ objections to natural agency must be disaggregated: denial of necessary conjunction, denial of independent power, and denial of intrinsic efficacy are not equivalent.
chapters.AT: Aquinas objects to an Avicennian separate giver of substantial forms and affirms substantial generation through natural agents while maintaining divine dependence. That cannot be imported merely by affirming the four causes.
chapters.open: The relevant Tajrīd locus is the debate over corporeal powers, to be expanded beyond the first fascicle. This chapter’s classical-textual coverage remains preliminary and is marked as such.
chapters.comparison: Al-Taftāzānī describes the dividing line: immediate divine production without natural efficacy versus philosophy’s spatially restricted natural operations. Qūshjī’s qualifications about conditions leave open whether natural agents are intrinsically productive. Aertsen’s AT account requires more: not only reliable conjunction or preparatory activities, but a determinate operation that truly belongs to the secondary agent.

chapters.title: Creation, conservation, concurrence, and secondary causality
chapters.question: How can a cause be wholly divine at one explanatory level and genuinely created at another?
chapters.evidence: Differentiate the efficient production of a being, its conservation, God’s immediate operation in created actions, and the natural agent’s own production. Islamic philosophical material already knows primary and secondary causes; the full Thomistic integration is not established by this vocabulary alone. The Māturīdī, Juwaynī, and later Akbarī theological reconstructions require their own arguments and cannot be inserted wholesale into Ṭūsī’s text.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s crucial claim is that the form is an intrinsic medium of natural being, whereas God is the immediate creative efficient cause of esse. This is a strong diagnostic against two causes competing horizontally.
chapters.open: A serious compatibility test must ask whether the natural cause is ontologically distinct and genuinely active, whether divine causation is immediate, and whether the same effect is non-competitively attributable to both.
chapters.comparison: Al-Taftāzānī’s defence of a freely specifying eternal will resists the demand that every temporal effect must require an additional new condition. Al-Jurjānī’s theological literature strongly distinguishes divine wisdom from a goal that perfects God. This does not by itself resolve the Aquinas-inspired distinction between the divine cause of *being as such* and the creature’s proper operation. Keep creation, conservation, and concurrence conceptually separate.

chapters.title: Simplicity, emanation, the First Intellect, and one-from-one
chapters.arabic: الواحد لا يصدر عنه إلا الواحد
chapters.question: How can one simple First Principle explain a world of multiple differentiated effects?
chapters.evidence: Ḥillī criticizes attempts to derive multiplicity from aspects of the First Intellect. Qūshjī analyzes the proof and asks whether the rule holds without qualification. Qūnawī challenges the sufficiency of conceptual respects and proposes a different relation between one overflowing existence and differentiated receptivities. Ṭūsī’s response is more qualified than an unbounded one-from-one slogan.
chapters.AT: AT distinguishes the simplicity of God from an emanation ordered through necessary intermediary creators. Compare the causality of being itself with the division into many natural forms and exemplary reasons.
chapters.open: Do not treat Akbarī taʿayyun, Illuminationist lights, and Thomistic participation as synonymous solutions. Each has a different ontology of plurality.
chapters.comparison: Al-Ḥillī critiques the multiplication of aspects in the First Intellect. Qūshjī scrutinizes the principle’s premise and regress arguments; Lāhījī offers a more qualified defence. In correspondence Qūnawī questions the explanatory basis of derived multiplicity, and Ṭūsī formulates one-from-one in respect-specific terms. These are disagreements about causal scope, not straightforward endorsements or denials of divine simplicity.

chapters.title: Divine knowledge, the intelligibility of forms, and exemplarity
chapters.question: How can God know individual things without receiving forms or losing simplicity?
chapters.evidence: The Qūnawī–Ṭūsī exchange directly disputes what philosophical demonstration can show about God’s knowledge and distinguishes knowledge of temporal events from being subject to time. Shīrāzī’s commentary expounds Illuminationist presential knowledge by the Light of Lights, rejecting a picture in which material images are received into the divine essence.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s two truth-measures must be kept distinct: things measure human knowledge, while divine exemplary knowledge grounds the intelligibility of their forms. This is not the same question as whether divine knowledge receives representations.
chapters.open: The strongest comparison is among divine exemplary causality, Avicennian intelligible order, Ishrāqī illumination, and Akbarī disclosure; a specific ontological equivalence remains unproven.
chapters.comparison: Shīrāzī’s Illuminationist explanation of divine knowledge through presential manifestation is a sharp criticism of an account requiring representations within the divine essence. He also presses the difference between actually knowing a concomitant and knowing it only potentially. Ṭūsī’s exchange with Qūnawī, and Ṭihrānī’s account of truth, allow the problem of cognition to be connected with but not reduced to the question of the First Cause’s knowledge.

chapters.title: Final causality, providence, and the good
chapters.question: Can nature be directed to genuine ends without making God act from need?
chapters.evidence: Ṭūsī and the commentators distinguish the final cause’s priority as a reason from its posteriority as a realized effect. Theological objections to divine purposes often target a need accruing to the agent, rather than all wisdom or beneficial order in the effect. The special case of divine purposiveness must be distinguished from ordinary natural agency.
chapters.AT: Aertsen links the good with actuality, inclination, and the return of things to their principle. Compare this structure with ḥikma and gharaḍ rather than assuming every account of divine wisdom entails Thomistic final causes.
chapters.open: This chapter has strong conceptual support but needs additional full extracts from Mawāqif and Maqāṣid before firm historical consensus claims.
chapters.comparison: A final cause’s priority in explanation does not entail that it temporally precedes the effect. Yet the theological prohibition on a purpose which perfects God is not identical with denying benefits in His creation. The precise meanings of gharaḍ, ghāya, ḥikma, and maslaha are therefore decisive. The Thomistic account of divine goodness as end must be compared at this level of precision, rather than as a bare claim that “God acts for ends”.

chapters.title: Soul, faculties, cognition, and acquired perfections
chapters.question: How can knowledge and repeated operations perfect a real human capacity?
chapters.evidence: The Tajrīd and later sources differentiate perceptual and intellectual faculties, forms in the intellect, the relation of motion and imagination, and extraordinary intellectual activity. The Ṭihrānī passages on motion, mental existence, and quiddity are directly relevant; his later prophecy passage (p.644) remains an identified translation target.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s account relates soul–intellect–will to being–true–good. An AT–Islamic synthesis should proceed from the ontology of a faculty to its operation, acquired habit, and practical perfection.
chapters.open: This is the route toward malakāt, ethics, educational formation, and institutions, but it must not obscure disagreements over substantial soul, faculty ontologies, or intentional forms.
chapters.comparison: The earlier cognition passages treat ordinary representation, not all possible forms of immediate presence. Shīrāzī’s argument introduces a different mode of knowing; Ṭihrānī’s psychology of motion and imagination opens a further issue about the constitution of temporally extended objects in cognition. The later Akbarī distinction between acquired intellectual concepts and gifted disclosure should be tested only after separating these senses of presence.

chapters.title: Unveiling, demonstration, presence, and the knowledge of God
chapters.question: When can a spiritual disclosure count as knowledge, and how is it rationally assessed?
chapters.evidence: In the correspondence Qūnawī claims priority for knowledge of the Real through the Real. Ṭūsī praises this description of unveiling but continues to offer philosophical replies. Jurjānī’s direct Tajrīd glosses on waḥdat al-wujūd are verified as a separate textual cluster through Heer; the texts have not yet been fully translated in the preceding fascicles. Lāhījī explicitly reports a mystical indication and discusses objections.
chapters.AT: Compare Aquinas’s knowing the First Cause and Aertsen’s treatment of natural and supernatural perfection, while sharply distinguishing Christian theological grace, Islamic kashf, Ishrāqī knowledge by presence, and ordinary mental existence.
chapters.open: A rigorous assessment must identify a doctrine’s epistemic source, its demonstration, its hermeneutic rendering, and the limit of claimed certainty.
chapters.comparison: Here the direct exchange is unusually important: Qūnawī distinguishes knowing the Real through acquired intellectual faculties from knowing the Real through the Real. Ṭūsī praises this claim yet elsewhere protects philosophical reasoning as a distinct route. Jurjānī’s Taʿrīfāt entry is only a parallel, not the direct Ḥāshiyat al-Tajrīd mystical glosses. The latter are identified by Nicholas Heer, but their complete argumentative units still require primary collation.

chapters.title: Unity of existence, determinations, lights, and created reality
chapters.question: Are creatures distinct beings, determinations of one existence, or ordered manifestations?
chapters.evidence: Qūnawī and Ṭūsī debate the status of existence and possible quiddities. Jāmī frames a comparison of philosophical, theological, and Sufi approaches. Fanārī distinguishes dependence through intermediaries from the direct “particular face.” Dawwānī and Dashtakī preserve adjacent Illuminationist questions, not a complete one-to-one debate on one lemma. Jurjānī and Lāhījī must be read with attribution controls.
chapters.AT: Aertsen’s participation and created subject–essence–esse provide a possible comparator, but do not license identification with Akbarī taʿayyunāt or Illuminationist immaterial lights.
chapters.open: Study the objective distinction of creatures, the efficacy of natural powers, the nature of universal existence, and the role of spiritual witnessing as independent tests.
chapters.comparison: The unity-of-existence issue must be built from actual exchanges. Qūnawī’s objections, Ṭūsī’s differentiated predication, Jāmī’s comparative account, Fanārī’s special face, and the Dawwānī–Dashtakī Illuminationist controversy do not represent one doctrinal school. The outstanding Jurjānī Ḥāshiya glosses and Lāhījī’s complete Ishāra ʿirfāniyya are particularly important gaps. None should be silently replaced by a lexicon entry or a report from later scholarship.

extracts.title: The boundary between being and thingness
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “Existence is coextensive with thingness [الشيئية]; thingness is not realized without it, and anyone who disputes this defies what his own intellect requires.”
I say: Whoever holds that existence [الوجود] is identical with quiddity [الماهية] cannot say that the nonexistent is a thing in the sense that a quiddity can be established outside the mind while separated from existence. Otherwise, the two contradictories—existence and nonexistence—would obtain together.
Those who hold that existence is additional to quiddity disagree among themselves. Some maintain that a quiddity can be established extramentally while separated from existence. This is what they mean by “the nonexistent is a thing” [المعدوم شيء]. Others deny it. The former is the position of the Muʿtazila; the latter, that of the remaining theologians and philosophers.
On this interpretation, they agree that what is absolutely excluded [المنفي] is not a thing: by this they mean quiddities whose extramental existence is impossible. The real dispute therefore concerns nonexistent quiddities that are possible of existence.
Ṭūsī's statement that existence is coextensive with thingness means that whatever exists is a thing, and whatever does not exist is not a thing. Thus something nonexistent outside the mind—whether its existence is possible or impossible—is not an extramental thing.
extracts.arabic:
قال: ويساوق الشيئية فلا تتحقق بدونه، والمنازع مكابر مقتضى عقله.
أقول: اعلم أن من قال بأن الوجود عين الماهية لا يمكنه القول بكون المعدوم شيئًا، على معنى أن الماهية يجوز تقررها في الخارج منفكة عن الوجود؛ وإلا لزم اجتماع النقيضين، وهو الوجود والعدم معًا.
وأما من قال بأن الوجود زائد على الماهية فقد اختلفوا: فزعم بعضهم أن الماهية يجوز تقررها في الخارج منفكة عن الوجود، وهذا معنى قولهم «المعدوم شيء»، ومنهم من منع ذلك. والأول مذهب المعتزلة، والثاني مذهب سائر المتكلمين والحكماء.
واتفقوا على أن المنفي ليس بشيء على هذا التفسير، وعنوا بالمنفي الماهيات الممتنعة الوجود في الخارج، فعلى هذا محل النزاع الماهيات المعدومة الممكنة الوجود.
إذا عرفت ذلك فاعلم أن قوله «ويساوق الشيئية» أي الوجود يساوق الشيئية ويلازمها، على معنى أن كل ما هو موجود فهو شيء، وكل ما ليس بموجود فهو ليس بشيء؛ فالمعدوم في الخارج، سواء كان ممكنًا أو ممتنعًا، ليس بشيء.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  The dispute is narrower than whether the intellect can conceive or speak about the nonexistent. The opposed claim is an extramental establishment [تقرر في الخارج] of a possible quiddity without existence. “Coextensive” [مساوق] does not mean that the concepts are synonymous.

extracts.title: Two senses of establishment in the Muʿtazilī thesis
extracts.english:
The Muʿtazilī position is that establishment [التقرر] has two kinds. The first is a quiddity's establishment in itself [في حد ذاتها]; the second is its establishment in such a way that its effects follow from it, as burning follows from fire and moistening from water. They call the first “establishment” [الثبوت], opposed to exclusion or negation [النفي], and the second “existence” [الوجود], opposed to nonexistence [العدم].
They sometimes use “nonexistence” for “exclusion” as well. They permit establishment to accompany either existence or its opposite, nonexistence. If “the nonexistent has no establishment” means the first kind, it is denied—and alleging that the opponent is defying reason is itself unwarranted. If it means the second kind, it is granted. But the disagreement concerns the first.
extracts.arabic: مذهب المعتزلة أن التقرر على ضربين: تقرر الماهية في حد ذاتها، وتقررها بحيث يترتب عليها آثارها، كإحراق النار وترطيب الماء؛ فالأول يسمونه ثبوتًا ومقابله نفيًا، والثاني يسمونه وجودًا ومقابله عدمًا. وقد يطلقون العدم على النفي أيضًا، ويجوزون اجتماع الثبوت مع كل واحد من الوجود والعدم المقابل له. فإن أراد بقوله «المعدوم لا تقرر له» المعنى الأول فهو ممنوع، ودعوى المكابرة مكابرة؛ وإن أراد المعنى الثاني فهو مسلم، وإنما النزاع في المعنى الأول.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  Jurjānī's gloss is methodological: one cannot refute the opponent by shifting from the disputed sense of thubūt to the conceded sense of effect-bearing wujūd. The translated passage is confined to the clear initial argument of the gloss, not its complete subsequent treatment.

extracts.title: Thingness as a second intelligible
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “Thingness [الشيئية] belongs to the second intelligibles [المعقولات الثانية]. It does not have an independent foundation in existence. No thingness taken absolutely is established; rather, it attaches to particular quiddities.”
I say: Abū ʿAlī Ibn Sīnā said that existence is either mental or extramental, and that thingness is common to both. If he meant that thingness can be predicated of what is common to them and applies to it, this is correct. If he meant something else, it is not conceded.
Thingness, essentiality [الذاتية], particularity [الجزئية], and similar notions are second intelligibles attaching to first intelligibles. They cannot be conceived except as belonging to other quiddities. They do not have an independent foundation in existence in the way animality and humanity do; rather, they depend upon something else for their existence. There can be no thingness existing absolutely. It is not thingness as such that is established; establishment belongs to specifically determined quiddities.
extracts.arabic:
قال: والشيئية من المعقولات الثانية وليست متأصلة في الوجود، فلا شيء مطلقًا ثابت بل هي تعرض لخصوصيات الماهيات.
أقول: قال أبو علي بن سينا: الوجود إما ذهني وإما خارجي، والمشترك بينهما هو الشيئية. فإن أراد حمل الشيئية على القدر المشترك وصدقها عليه فهو صواب، وإلا فهو ممنوع.
إذا عرفت هذا فنقول: الشيئية والذاتية والجزئية وأشباهها من المعقولات الثانية التي تعرض للمعقولات الأولى؛ لأنها لا تعقل إلا عارضة لغيرها من الماهيات، وليست متأصلة في الوجود كتأصل الحيوانية والإنسانية فيه، بل هي تابعة لغيرها في الوجود. وليس يمكن وجود شيئية مطلقة؛ فلا شيء مطلقًا ثابت، إنما الثبوت يعرض للماهيات المخصوصة الشخصية.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  The sense of “second intelligible” here is metaphysical and must not be silently identified with the narrower logical sense. The modern Āmulī footnote develops the distinction at length; that later explanation is not part of al-Ḥillī's medieval text.

extracts.title: Predication of the nonexistent and the objection from heat
extracts.section: II. Mental existence and the object of knowledge
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “Existence is divided into mental [الذهني] and extramental [الخارجي]; otherwise, the real or universally quantified proposition [القضية الحقيقية] would fail.”
I say: Rational inquirers differ on this question. One group denies mental existence [الوجود الذهني] and confines existence to what is extramental; the investigators affirm it and recognize a genuine division into extramental and mental existence. Ṭūsī argues that a real proposition is certainly true, since we affirm predicates of subjects that have no existence among extramental individuals. A property's obtaining requires its subject to obtain. Since such a subject is not established extramentally, it is realized mentally.
Ṭūsī says: “What exists in the mind is only the form [الصورة], which differs from the thing in many of its concomitants.”
This answers the argument of those who deny mental existence. They argue: if a quiddity came to be in the mind, the mind would have to be hot and cold, black and white; the mind would then possess incompatible attributes, and contradictories would be combined. The answer is that what occurs in the mind is not heat and blackness as extramental realities, but their forms or representations, which differ from the quiddities in their consequences and properties. Extramental heat entails hotness; its mental form does not. Opposition belongs to the realities, not to their forms and representations.
extracts.arabic:
قال: وهو ينقسم إلى الذهني والخارجي وإلا لبطلت الحقيقية.
أقول: اختلف العقلاء هاهنا؛ فجماعة منهم نفوا الوجود الذهني وحصروا الوجود في الخارجي، والمحققون منهم أثبتوه وقسموا الوجود إلى الخارجي والذهني قسمة حقيقية. واستدل المصنف بأن القضية الحقيقية صادقة قطعًا؛ لأنا نحكم بالأحكام الإيجابية على موضوعات معدومة في الأعيان، وتحقق الصفة يستدعي تحقق الموصوف، وإذ ليس ثابتًا في الأعيان فهو متحقق في الذهن.
قال: والموجود في الذهن إنما هو الصورة المخالفة في كثير من اللوازم.
أقول: هذا جواب عن استدلال من نفى الوجود الذهني، وتقرير استدلالهم أنه لو حلت الماهية في الأذهان لزم أن يكون الذهن حارًا باردًا أسود أبيض، فيلزم مع اتصاف الذهن بهذه الأشياء المنفية عنه اجتماع الضدين. والجواب أن الحاصل في الذهن ليس هو ماهية الحرارة والسواد بل صورتهما ومثالهما المخالفة للماهية في لوازمها وأحكامها، فالحرارة الخارجية تستلزم السخونة وصورتها لا تستلزمها، والتضاد إنما هو بين الماهيات لا بين صورها وأمثلتها.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  The phrase qaḍiyya ḥaqīqiyya is a technical term of the logic of propositions, not a vague “true statement.” The argument from positive predication needs separate scrutiny: it may rely on a controversial principle concerning the existence of the subject. This is an al-Ḥillī translation, not proof that all later accounts endorse “likenesses” rather than presence of quiddities.
extracts.source_line: Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī  |  Kashf al-murād, discussion of mental existence; al-Zanjānī recension, p. 19 (also Āmulī ed. around pp. 39–40). | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3438/19?lang=ar

extracts.title: Knowledge as a psychic quality; the known as a universal
extracts.section: II. Mental existence and the object of knowledge
extracts.english:
On the basis of our analysis, we say this: when the concept of animal [مفهوم الحيوان], for example, occurs in the mind, then insofar as it inheres in the mind as a psychic quality [كيفية نفسانية], it is knowledge [العلم] of that concept. In that respect it is an accident [عرض] and a particular [جزئي], because it inheres in an individual soul and is individuated by mental individuating features; in that respect it is something extramentally existent.
What is mentally existent, however, is the concept of animal as occurring in the mind. This is a universal [كلي], a substance [جوهر], and an object known [معلوم].
extracts.arabic: وعلى تحقيقنا هذا نقول: إن مفهوم الحيوان مثلًا إذا حصل في الذهن، فحيث يقوم بالذهن كيفية نفسانية هو العلم بهذا المفهوم، وهو عرض وجزئي لكونه قائمًا بنفس شخصي، ومشخصًا بشخصيات ذهنية، وهو الموجود في الخارج. وأما الموجود في الذهن فهو مفهوم الحيوان الحاصل في الذهن، وهو كلي وجوهر ومعلوم.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  Qūshjī distinguishes the intentional or predicative status of what is known from the ontological status of the act/quality of knowing. The case presses the problem of how one cognitive occurrence can support categorial descriptions that seem incompatible. The text has been checked against the scanned Arabic page; the printed edition's surrounding glosses must not be conflated with his main text.

extracts.title: Three objections to mental existence, and the distinction that answers them
extracts.section: II. Mental existence and the object of knowledge
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī's statement that what exists in the mind is a form differing in many of its concomitants points to the answer to the arguments of those who deny mental existence [الوجود الذهني]. They constitute the majority of the theologians, although some theologians affirm it. Because the thesis depends on thought entailing mental existence and on the mentally existent inhering in the mind, its opponents concentrate their objections on these claims.
First: if conceiving a thing entailed its occurrence in the intellect, then conceiving heat and cold, straightness and curvature, would make the mind hot and cold, straight and curved. This is impossible: it would combine opposites and attribute to the mind properties belonging to bodies.
Second: it would follow that the heavens, with their immense size, would occur in the intellect when understood and in imagination when imagined. This is necessarily false.
Third: it would follow from thinking about nonexistent things that they exist outside the mind, because they exist in an intellect which itself exists outside the mind. Whatever exists in something that exists in a place also exists in that place—as water in a jug located in a house is in the house.
All three objections rest on failing to distinguish independently realized existence [الوجود المتأصل], through which an individual extramental reality subsists, from non-independent existence, through which there is an intellectual form. What possesses heat is that in which the extramental reality of heat subsists, not that in which its form occurs. Opposition holds between the extramental realities of heat and cold, not between their intellectual forms.
extracts.arabic:
والموجود في الذهن إنما هو الصورة المخالفة في كثير من اللوازم، إشارة إلى الجواب عن متمسكات النافين للوجود الذهني، وهم جمهور المتكلمين، فإن بعضهم قائلون به. ولما كان مبنى الوجود الذهني على استلزام التعقل إياه وقيام الموجود الذهني بالذهن اقتصر المانعون على نفيه بوجوه.
الأول: لو كان تصور الشيء مستلزمًا لحصوله في العقل، لزم من تصور الحرارة والبرودة والاستقامة والاعوجاج أن يكون الذهن حارًا باردًا مستقيمًا معوجًا، وهو محال لما فيه من اجتماع الضدين واتصاف الذهن بما هو من خواص الأجسام.
الثاني: أنه يلزم أن تحصل السماوات مثلًا بعظمها في العقل عند تعقلها، وفي الخيال عند تخيلها، وهو باطل بالضرورة.
الثالث: أنه يلزم من تعقلنا للمعدومات وجودها في الخارج، لكونها موجودة في العقل الموجود في الخارج، مع القطع بأن الموجود في الموجود في الشيء موجود في ذلك الشيء، كالماء الموجود في الكوز الموجود في البيت.
والجواب عن الكل أنه مبني على عدم التفرقة بين الوجود المتأصل الذي به الهوية العينية، وغير المتأصل الذي به الصورة العقلية. فإن المتصف بالحرارة مثلًا ما يقوم به هوية الحرارة لا صورتها، والتضاد إنما هو بين هويتي الحرارة والبرودة لا بين صورتيهما.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  Lāhījī here gives the objections considerable force, then restricts the supposed transfer of extramental properties to mental representations. Later pages introduce further difficulties involving categories, the object of knowledge, and Dawwānī's alternative. Those continuations require their own translation and are not silently included here.

extracts.title: Why the ground of need must be possibility rather than origination
extracts.section: III. Possibility, origination, and causal need
extracts.english:
There has been disagreement concerning the ground of an effect's need for its efficient cause [علة احتياج الأثر إلى مؤثره]. The majority of rational inquirers maintain that it is possibility [الإمكان] alone; others, temporal origination [الحدوث] alone; still others, both together. The first position is correct for two reasons.
First: when the intellect considers a possible quiddity [ماهية ممكنة] and seeks to predicate existence or nonexistence of it, it requires a cause, without considering anything beyond its possibility and the equal standing of the alternatives. The intellect's judgment of intrinsic equality is sufficient to rule out an intrinsic preponderance of one alternative. Accordingly, the thing needs a cause insofar as it is possible, without further consideration. Suppose that something that began to exist had necessary existence—even though this supposition is impossible. The intellect would judge that it did not need an efficient cause. The ground of need is therefore possibility alone.
Second: temporal origination is a qualification of existence [كيفية الوجود], and is posterior to existence in the order of intrinsic dependence. Existence is posterior to the bringing-about of existence [الإيجاد]; bringing-about is posterior to need [الاحتياج]; and need is posterior to the ground of need. If temporal origination were the ground of need, the same thing would have to precede itself by several stages. That is impossible.
extracts.arabic:
أقول: اختلف الناس هنا في علة احتياج الأثر إلى مؤثره، فقال جمهور العقلاء: إنها الإمكان لا غير، وقال آخرون: إنها الحدوث لا غير، وقال آخرون: هما معًا. والحق الأول لوجهين.
الأول: العقل إذا لحظ الماهية الممكنة وأراد حمل الوجود أو العدم عليها افتقر في ذلك إلى العلة، وإن لم ينظر شيئًا آخر سوى الإمكان والتساوي؛ إذ حكم العقل بالتساوي الذاتي كاف في الحكم بامتناع الرجحان الذاتي، فاحتاج إلى العلة من حيث هو ممكن وإن لم يلحظ غيره. ولو فرضنا حادثًا وجب وجوده، وإن كان فرضًا محالًا، فإن العقل يحكم بعدم احتياجه إلى المؤثر، فعلم أن علة الحاجة إنما هي الإمكان لا غير.
الثاني: أن الحدوث كيفية للوجود فيتأخر عنه تأخرًا ذاتيًا، والوجود متأخر عن الإيجاد، والإيجاد متأخر عن الاحتياج، والاحتياج متأخر عن علة الاحتياج. فلو كان الحدوث علة الحاجة لزم تقدم الشيء على نفسه بمراتب، وهو محال.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  Ḥillī does not infer that every possible being began in time. His argument isolates the basis of dependence; the temporal status of the world remains a further issue. Likewise “necessary” here concerns necessity of existence [وجوب الوجود], not immediate knowledge [علم ضروري].
extracts.source_line: Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī  |  Kashf al-murād, ed. Āmulī, p. 78 (complete two-argument reply within the selected issue). | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3439/78?lang=ar
extracts.author: al-Ḥillī

extracts.title: The persistent possible continues to need its cause
extracts.section: III. Possibility, origination, and causal need
extracts.english:
“The ground of need for an efficient cause [علة الحاجة إلى المؤثر] is possibility [الإمكان], as has already been shown, not temporal origination [الحدوث]. For origination is a qualification [كيفية] of the existence of an originated thing, and is therefore posterior to it.”

“The possible [الممكن] does not dispense with an efficient cause while it persists [حال بقائه]. For the ground of need is possibility, and possibility necessarily accompanies the possible quiddity [الماهية الممكنة]. Therefore it stands in need at all times.”
extracts.arabic:
علة الحاجة إلى المؤثر الإمكان لما سبق لا الحدوث؛ لأن الحدوث كيفية لوجود الحادث فيكون متأخرًا عنه.

والممكن حال بقائه لا يستغني عن المؤثر؛ لأن علة الحاجة الإمكان، والإمكان ضروري اللزوم للماهية الممكنة، فهي أبدًا محتاجة.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  These are two separate brief quotations from Rāzī's Muḥaṣṣal, juxtaposed for comparison and not represented as a continuous paragraph. The necessity conveyed by ḍarūrī al-luzūm [ضروري اللزوم] concerns the necessary concomitance of a property with a quiddity—not the epistemic classification of immediate knowledge [العلم الضروري]. Rāzī is a comparative predecessor here, not a commentator on Ṭūsī's later Tajrīd. He distinguishes necessary dependence from temporal beginning; that distinction is not equivalent to affirming an eternal world.
extracts.source_line: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (comparative primary source, not a Tajrīd commentator)  |  Al-Muḥaṣṣal, text printed pp. 206–207 (two short, non-contiguous statements; modern editorial introduction also quotes them). | Arabic source: https://books.rafed.net/view/3639/page/206
extracts.author: al-Rāzī

extracts.title: The four explanatory causes and their extra conditions
extracts.section: IV. What the four causes do—and do not—explain
extracts.english:
Of the internal causes, one may be that through which the effect exists potentially [بالقوة]: this is the material cause [العلة المادية], as wood is in relation to a bed. Or it may be that through which it exists actually [بالفعل]: this is the formal cause [العلة الصورية], as the form of the bed is in relation to it.
As for the external causes, either existence proceeds from a cause or existence is for its sake. The former is the efficient cause [العلة الفاعلية], as the carpenter is in relation to the bed; the latter is the final cause [العلة الغائية], as sitting on the bed is in relation to it. Conditions [الشرائط] and the removal of impediments [ارتفاع الموانع] are referred back to completing the material or efficient cause.
extracts.arabic: والأولى إما أن يكون المعلول به بالقوة، وهي العلة المادية، كالخشب بالنسبة إلى السرير؛ أو بالفعل، وهي العلة الصورية، كصورة السرير بالنسبة إليه. والخارجية إما أن يكون منها الوجود أو لأجلها الوجود؛ والأولى هي العلة الفاعلية، كالنجار بالنسبة إلى السرير، والثانية الغائية، كالجلوس على السرير بالنسبة إليه. وأما الشرائط وارتفاع الموانع فراجعة إلى تتميم العلة المادية أو الفاعلية.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  This is a classification of explanations, not yet a defence of prime matter, corporeal substantial forms, or a necessary emanation from God. Potentiality [قوة] here is opposed to actuality [فعل]; it must not be translated as power [قدرة].
extracts.source_line: Shams al-Dīn al-Iṣfahānī  |  Tasdīd al-qawāʿid, İSAM vol. II, printed pp. 354–355 (selected closing division of the causes). | Arabic source: https://archive.org/download/tsdidqawaed/tqat2.pdf
extracts.author: al-Iṣfahānī

extracts.title: The distinction between causes of quiddity and causes of existence
extracts.section: IV. What the four causes do—and do not—explain
extracts.english:
Know that causes entering into the constitution [قوام] of an effect are called causes of quiddity [علل الماهية], while those external to it are called causes of existence [علل الوجود]. This indicates that the first class is required by quiddity just as it is required by existence, whereas the second is required by existence but not by quiddity.
An objection may be raised: the internal causes—that is, the parts of the quiddity—are not exhausted by the material and the formal. Genus [الجنس] and differentia [الفصل] are also parts of the quiddity, yet neither is a material cause nor a formal cause.
extracts.arabic:
واعلم أن العلل الداخلة في قوام المعلول تسمّى علل الماهية، والخارجة عنه تسمّى علل الوجود، تنبيهًا على أن القسم الأول يتوقف عليه الماهية كما يتوقف عليه الوجود، وأن القسم الثاني يتوقف عليه الوجود دون الماهية.
وربما يقال: إن العلل الداخلة، أعني أجزاء الماهية، لا تنحصر في المادية والصورية؛ لأن الجنس والفصل من أجزاء الماهية، وليس شيء منهما صورة ولا مادة.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  The gloss does not merely deny fourfold causation. It asks whether the kinds of “part” relevant to definition (genus and differentia) can be subsumed under causes of a concrete thing (matter and form). Jurjānī's continuation develops a reply; only this stated objection is translated here.
extracts.source_line: Al-Sayyid al-Sharīf al-Jurjānī  |  Ḥāshiya in Tasdīd, İSAM vol. II, printed p. 355 (initial paragraph of a longer critique). | Arabic source: https://archive.org/download/tsdidqawaed/tqat2.pdf
extracts.author: al-Jurjānī

extracts.title: How a final cause can be prior and posterior
extracts.section: IV. What the four causes do—and do not—explain
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “The end [الغاية], in respect of its quiddity, is the cause of the efficient cause's being a cause; in respect of its existence, it is an effect of what is produced.”
I say: An end has two aspects, by virtue of which it is prior and posterior to the effect. The agent first conceives the end, acts, and only then does the end come to exist when the action has produced its result. Thus the quiddity of the end is a cause of the efficient cause's causal activity: without that quiddity and its occurrence in the agent's knowledge, the agent would not bring about the action. Someone building a house first conceives shelter, then proceeds to construct the house; when the house exists, shelter comes to be available. The quiddity of shelter thus explains the agent's activity, while shelter's existence is consequent upon the house. There is no impossibility in the same thing being prior and posterior in two different respects.
extracts.arabic:
قال: والغاية علة بماهيتها لعلية العلة الفاعلية، معلولة في وجودها للمعلول.
أقول: الغاية لها اعتباران يحصل لها باعتبارهما التقدم والتأخر بالنسبة إلى المعلول؛ وذلك لأن الفاعل إذا تصور الغاية فعل الفعل ثم حصلت الغاية بحصول الفعل. فماهية الغاية علة لعلية الفاعل؛ إذ لولا تلك الماهية وحصولها في علم الفاعل لما أثر ولا فعل الفعل. فإن الفاعل للبيت يتصور الاستكنان أولًا فيتحرك إلى إيجاد البيت، ثم يوجد الاستكنان بحصول البيت. فماهية الاستكنان علة لعلية الفاعل ووجوده معلول للبيت؛ ولا امتناع في أن يكون الشيء الواحد متقدمًا ومتأخرًا باعتبارين.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  “Cause” changes explanatory sense across the sentence: an end as conceived can motivate the productive action, while the end's realization follows the completed product. This is not an argument that every agent, including God, acts to gain a perfection.
extracts.source_line: Al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī  |  Kashf al-murād, ed. Āmulī, p. 198, discussion of the final cause. | Arabic source: https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/3439/198?lang=ar
extracts.author: al-Ḥillī

extracts.title: Conditions, instruments and impediments: does the fourfold list exhaust causal need?
extracts.section: IV. What the four causes do—and do not—explain
extracts.english:
An objection is made: we have said that “efficient cause” means what is independently effective, and “matter” means what is actually receptive. Yet the effect also requires each of the things just mentioned [conditions, instruments, and the removal of obstacles]. None of them, however, is properly described as a part of the effect, that from which it is made, or that for whose sake it exists. To say that the division is not exhaustive means only that something falls under the divided subject without belonging to any of its proposed divisions.
One may reply that an effect requires, in the first instance, a recipient actually capable of receiving and an independently acting efficient cause. Its requirement for the other items is secondary, mediated by the dependence of those two causes upon them. They would thus be causes through an intermediary [علل بالواسطة], whereas the subject of the division is the immediate cause of a thing [علة الشيء بلا واسطة].
I say: a difficulty nevertheless remains. The final cause should then have been counted as part of what completes the efficient cause, since they maintain that the end affects the efficient cause's very exercise of causality.
extracts.arabic:
ورد بأنّا قد قلنا: إن المراد بالفاعل هو المستقل بالفاعلية، وبالمادة هو القابل بالفعل، لكن كلًّا مما ذكر يحتاج إليه المعلول، ولا يصدق عليه أنه جزء للمعلول، ولا ما منه، ولا ما لأجله؛ ولا نعني بعدم الحصر في الأقسام إلا وجود شيء يصدق عليه المقسم ولا يصدق عليه شيء من الأقسام.
ويمكن دفعه بأن المراد أن المعلول يحتاج أولًا إلى القابل بالفعل والفاعل بالاستقلال، واحتياجه إلى ما ذكر إنما هو ثانيًا وبواسطة احتياجهما إليها، فتكون تلك المذكورات من العلل بالواسطة، والمقسم هو علة الشيء بلا واسطة.
أقول: لكن يبقى شيء، وهو أنه كان يجب أن تجعل العلة الغائية من تتمة الفاعل؛ لأنهم قالوا إن الغاية مؤثرة في مؤثرية الفاعل.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  The opening presents an objection and a possible reply, not an unqualified statement of Qūshjī's own final commitment. The “I say” at the end marks Qūshjī's further criticism. The later printed note of Dawwānī, not translated here, presses an additional distinction concerning final causality.

extracts.title: The First Intellect and the failure of merely relational multiplicity
extracts.section: V. The one-from-one principle and its limits
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “Multiplicity then supervenes by reason of a multiplicity of relations [الإضافات].”
I say: Once it had been established that only one effect proceeds from one cause, it would follow that all existing things formed a single chain, so that any two things whatever would stand to one another as cause and effect, directly or indirectly. There could then be no two things independent of one another. But actuality contradicts this. The philosophers therefore posited a multiplicity in the first effect—not a real multiplicity, but one of relations—through which its causal activity could be diversified.
They say that the first effect is possible [ممكن] when considered in itself but necessary [واجب] in relation to its cause; it possesses a quiddity and an existence received from its agent; and, being immaterial, it knows itself and its principle. These form a multiplicity of relational respects that do not compromise its unity, and from each respect something proceeds.
We regard this argument as profoundly unsatisfactory. These respects are incapable of exercising causal influence: they are merely conceptual considerations [أمور اعتبارية], comparable to other such considerations, and cannot function as conditions of the effect.
extracts.arabic:
قال: ثم تعرض الكثرة باعتبار كثرة الإضافات.
أقول: لما بيّن أن العلة الواحدة لا يصدر عنها إلا معلول واحد، لزم أن تكون الموجودات بأسرها في سلسلة واحدة، بحيث يكون أي موجود فرضته علة لأي موجود فرضته أو معلولًا له، إما قريبة أو بعيدة، فلا يوجد شيئان يستغني أحدهما عن الآخر، والوجود يكذب هذا. فأوجبوا وقوع كثرة في المعلول الأول غير حقيقية بل إضافية يمكن أن يتكثر بها التأثير.
قالوا: لأن المعلول الأول بالنظر إلى ذاته ممكن، وبالنظر إلى علته واجب، وله ماهية ووجود مستفاد من فاعله، وهو يعقل ذاته لتجرده ويعقل مبدأه؛ وهذه جهات كثيرة إضافية يقع بها التكثر ولا تثلم وحدته، ويصدر عنه باعتبار كل جهة شيء.
وهذا الكلام عندنا في غاية السقوط، لأن هذه الجهات لا تصلح للتأثير؛ لأنها أمور اعتبارية ومساوية لغيرها ولا تكون شروطًا فيه.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  This is a targeted criticism of the proposed transition from the First Intellect to the multiplicity of the cosmos; it is not by itself a formal proof against every possible one-from-one principle. The extensive metaphysical footnote in the Āmulī edition is the modern editor's, not al-Ḥillī's.

extracts.title: The scope of the rule and a challenge to its demonstration
extracts.section: V. The one-from-one principle and its limits
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “When the cause is one, its effect is one.”
I say: If an agent is one in its essence, has no [additional] attribute, and its activity is not conditional upon anything else, the philosophers hold that more than one effect cannot proceed from it. Most theologians disagree. One might claim that its impossibility in the case of an agent acting by the necessity of its nature [الموجب بالذات], and its possibility in the case of a voluntary agent [الفاعل المختار], are both agreed upon, and that the real dispute is simply whether the First Principle is necessary or voluntary.
The correct point is that a voluntary agent whose acts of will or their objects are multiple, as the theologians maintain, falls outside the present case. Such an agent has multiplicity in respect of its acts of will or their relations, and so is not one in every respect.
The philosophers offer several proofs. The first is this: if something absolutely one were the source of two effects, its being-source of the first [مصدريته لهذا] would differ from its being-source of the second. If each were identical with the absolutely one, the same thing would have two distinct realities; but if either entered into its constitution, composition would follow, and it would not be absolutely one.
[The further alternative, where the respects are external to the First, is omitted here.]
One response is to turn the argument back upon its own notion of sourcehood [المصدرية]. If the demonstration were valid, the same problem would arise with the cause's being-a-source: when something proceeds from what is absolutely one, its sourcehood for that effect is a relational property differing from it, since it is a relation between two distinct things. This property must either enter into the cause—entailing composition—or be an effect external to it. In the latter case we must ask about the cause's sourcehood of that relation, and so on without end.
extracts.arabic:
قال: ومع وحدته يتحد المعلول.
أقول: الفاعل إذا كان واحدًا في ذاته، ولم يكن له صفة، ولم يكن فعله مشروطًا بأمر، لم يجز عند الحكماء أن يصدر عنه أكثر من واحد، خلافًا لأكثر المتكلمين. وقد يزعم أن عدم جواز ذلك في الموجب بالذات وجوازه في الفاعل المختار، وكلاهما متفق عليه، وإنما النزاع بينهم في أن المبدأ الأول موجب أو مختار.
والحق أن الفاعل المختار إذا تعددت إراداته أو تعلقاتها، على ما ذهب إليه المتكلمون، كان خارجًا عما نحن بصدده، إذ فيه كثرة باعتبار تعدد إراداته أو تعلقاتها، فلا يكون واحدًا من كل الوجوه.
احتج الحكماء بوجوه: الأول: لو كان الواحد الحقيقي مصدرًا لأمرين كانت مصدريته لهذا غير مصدريته لذاك؛ فإن كان كل واحد منهما نفس الواحد الحقيقي كان لأمر واحد حقيقتان مختلفتان، وإن دخل فيه واحد منهما لزم التركيب، فلم يكن واحدًا من جميع الوجوه.
[... حذف هنا فرع من البرهان يتعلق بفرض خروج الجهتين عن الذات ...]
وأجيب تارة بالنقض، وتقريره أنه لو تم هذا الدليل لزم مثله في صفة المصدريّة؛ فإنا نقول: لو صدر عن الواحد الحقيقي شيء، فمصدريته لذلك الشيء أمر مغاير له، لكونه نسبة بين غيرين، فهو إما داخل فيه فيلزم تركيبه، أو خارج عنه معلول له، فتنتقل المسألة إلى مصدرية هذه النسبة، حتى يتسلسل.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  Qūshjī does not simply replace the philosophical thesis with a bare denial. He first narrows the condition of “one in every respect”, including the possibility of multiple willing-relations, and then exposes a regress problem in the first proposed demonstration. The paragraph is one stage in a larger dispute. A bracketed editorial ellipsis marks an omitted alternative in the philosophers’ initial proof, rather than representing the response as immediately adjacent in the original. This selection does not imply a final verdict on the whole principle.

extracts.title: A qualified defence of the one-from-one principle
extracts.section: V. The one-from-one principle and its limits
extracts.english:
Ṭūsī says: “When the cause is one, its effect is one.”
I say: Among the principles is this: if an independently acting cause is one in every respect—containing neither a plurality of parts nor a plurality of existence and quiddity, possessing no real additional attribute outside the mind or additional conceptual attribute in the intellect, and having an act that does not depend on a condition, instrument, or recipient—then only one effect can proceed from it at a single level. This is the philosophers' view, against that of the theologians.
This is what Ṭūsī indicates when he says that unity of cause entails unity of effect. It applies whether the agent acts necessarily or acts voluntarily with a choice and will identical with its essence. Philosophers call the latter kind an agent acting by satisfaction or approval [الفاعل بالرضا]. If, by contrast, its will and choice are additional to its essence—the type they call an agent acting by intention [الفاعل بالقصد]—it falls outside the issue. Such an agent contains an actual duality, whether or not its acts of will or their objects are multiple, and is not one in every respect.
For its demonstration, Avicenna says in the Ishārāt: “The concept of a cause insofar as A necessarily proceeds from it is different from the concept of a cause insofar as B necessarily proceeds from it.” If two things necessarily proceed from what is one, they do so through two distinct respects, distinct in concept and in reality. These must either constitute the cause, be among its concomitants, or be distributed between the two.
extracts.arabic:
قال: ومع وحدته يتحد المعلول.
أقول: ومنها أن الفاعل المستقل إذا كان واحدًا من جميع الجهات، بحيث لا يكون فيه كثرة الأجزاء، ولا كثرة الوجود والماهية، ولا يكون متصفًا بصفة حقيقية زائدة في الخارج أو اعتبارية زائدة في العقل، ولا يتوقف فعله على شرط وآلة وقابل؛ فلا يمكن أن يصدر عنه في مرتبة واحدة إلا معلول واحد، على ما ذهب إليه الحكماء خلافًا للمتكلمين.
وإليه أشار بقوله «ومع وحدته يتحد المعلول»، سواء كان الفاعل موجبًا أو مختارًا اختياره وإرادته نفس ذاته؛ والحكماء يسمون لمثل هذا المختار الفاعل بالرضا. وأما إذا كانت إرادته واختياره زائدة على ذاته، وهو الذي يسمونه الفاعل بالقصد، فهو خارج عما نحن فيه؛ لأن فيه اثنينيّة بالفعل، سواء تعددت إرادته أو تعلقها أو لا، فلا يكون واحدًا من جميع الجهات.
وأما بيان ذلك فقال الشيخ في الإشارات: «تنبيه: مفهوم أن علة ما بحيث تجب عنها أ غير مفهوم أن علة ما بحيث يجب عنها ب». وإذا كان الواحد يجب عنه شيئان، فمن حيثيتين مختلفتي المفهوم مختلفتي الحقيقة، فإما أن يكونا من مقوماته، أو من لوازمه، أو بالتفريق.
notes: TRANSLATOR’S NOTE  This passage is a qualified rather than indiscriminate endorsement. The logical condition of the rule excludes a purportedly simple source with an additional willing-state, instrumental condition, or receptive substrate. The quotation from Avicenna is translated here as reported by Lāhījī, not independently collated against a critical Ishārāt edition.

extracts.title: Qūnawī’s trilemma: a common concept of existence
extracts.english:
First question. Has it been established, in your view, whether the existence of the Necessary Existent [واجب الوجود] is something additional [زائد] to His reality, or whether His existence is identical with His quiddity [ماهية], so that He has no reality beyond existence? What demonstration makes this clear? Everything advanced in support of either alternative seems incomplete and fails to satisfy a discerning mind.

Suppose, following the arguments of certain thinkers, one says that His existence is identical with His reality. An objector may reply: We do not concede this. One reason is that the concept of existence [مفهوم الوجود], as determined in our understanding, is plainly one concept. Consider it solely as itself, disregarding everything else. Either it entails being an accident or concomitant of a quiddity, or entails not being so, or entails neither.

On the first alternative, every instance of existence must belong to, or at least be capable of belonging to, a quiddity; hence the Necessary Existent’s existence would be an attribute of His reality. On the second, none of the conceived existences could belong to a quiddity: either possible quiddities do not exist, or their existence is identical with their respective realities. In that case, however, the concept of existence would not be one, contrary to our supposition. On the third, His existence would be independent of quiddity only through some distinct factor; He who is necessary through Himself would then be necessary through another. This too is contradictory.
extracts.arabic: المسألة الأولى: هل ثبت عندكم أنّ وجود واجب الوجود أمر زائد على حقيقته أم وجوده عين ماهيته وأن ليست له حقيقة وراء الوجود؟ وما البرهان الموضح تحقيق ذلك؟ فإنّ جميع ما ذكر في تقرير كل واحد من الأمرين غير تام ولا مقنع للّبيب، لأنه إن قيل بأنّ وجوده عين حقيقته اعتمادا ورضى بما ذكره جماعة في تقرير ذلك، فلقائل أن يقول: لا نسلّم أنّ وجود الحق عين حقيقته، ويدل على ذلك من وجوه. منها أنه من البيّن أنّ مفهوم الوجود من حيث تعيّنه في تعقّلنا مفهوم واحد. وهذا المفهوم من حيث إنه هو مع قطع النظر عن كل ما سواه إما أن يقتضي أن يكون عارضا لماهية شيء من الماهيات، أو يقتضي أن لا يكون عارضا لها، أو لا يقتضي واحدا من القسمين. فإن كان الأول، وجب أن يكون كل وجود عارضا لماهيته، أو له صلاحية ذلك. فوجود واجب الوجود يكون صفة لحقيقته. وإن كان الثاني، وجب أن لا يكون شيء من الوجودات المتعقّلة عارضا لشيء من الماهيات. فإما أن لا تكون هذه الماهيات الممكنة موجودة، أو تكون موجودة لكن وجودها نفس حقيقتها وحينئذ لا يكون مفهوم الوجود مفهوما واحدا. وقد فرضناه مفهوما واحدا. هذا خلف. وإن كان الثالث، فحينئذ لا يصير وجود واجب الوجود مجردا عن الماهية إلا لسبب منفصل، فيكون واجب الوجود لذاته واجب الوجود لغيره، هذا خلف.
notes: READING NOTE  Qūnawī’s argument depends upon a common conception being forced to have one uniform ontological consequence. Ṭūsī’s reply will deny precisely that inference by distinguishing univocal from graded predication.

extracts.title: Ṭūsī: the concept is common, the modes need not be uniform
extracts.english:
As for the demonstration that His existence is identical with His quiddity and that He has no reality beyond existence: if He possessed both existence and a distinct quiddity, the principle of all things would be two. Any two depend upon a unity that is their principle; whatever depends on a principle cannot itself be the principle of everything.

One might say that the quiddity is the qualified subject, and existence its qualification, so that the subject precedes its qualification and the first principle remains one—the quiddity. But if the quiddity precedes existence in this way, it is neither existent nor nonexistent; the principle of existents would therefore itself be nonexistent, which is impossible.

[In answer to the argument from one concept of existence:] Terms predicated of many things with one concept divide into two classes. First, the concept can apply equally to its instances, as “human” applies to Zayd and ʿAmr, or “horse” to these two horses. These terms are called univocal [متواطئة], and the requirements of their concepts are uniform, as you suggest.

Second, the concept may apply unequally—earlier or later, more properly or less properly, more intensely or less intensely. Examples include “white” as applied to snow and ivory, or “existent” as applied to substance and accident. Here the implications of the common concept need not be identical. “Light” is said of sunlight, moonlight, and firelight, yet sunlight dispels twilight in a way the others do not.

Existence [الوجود] belongs to this latter class. In the Necessary it subsists through itself, without inhering in a quiddity; in what is not necessary it is additional to a quiddity.
extracts.arabic:
أما البرهان الموضح تحقيق كون وجوده عين ماهيته وأن ليست له حقيقة وراء الوجود، فهو أنه لو كان له وجود وماهيته، لكان مبدأ الكل اثنين، وكل اثنين محتاج إلى واحد هو مبدأ الاثنين والمحتاج إلى مبدأ لا يكون مبدأ للكل. فإن قيل، الماهية موصوفة، والوجود صفة لها، والموصوف متقدم على الصفة القائمة بها، فالمبدأ الأول واحد وهو الماهية، قيل، الماهية على تقدير تقدمها على الوجود لا تكون موجودة ولا معدومة. وإذا يكون مبدأ الموجودات غير موجود، وهذا محال.

فجوابه: أنّ الألفاظ التي لها مفهوم واحد مقول على كثيرين تنقسم إلى قسمين: أحدهما أن يكون ذلك المفهوم في آحاد تلك الكثيرين بالسواء وهو كالإنسان في زيد وعمرو، والفرس في هذا الفرس وذلك الفرس. وتسمّى تلك الألفاظ بالمتواطئة، ويكون حكمها فيما تقتضي تلك المفهومات حكما واحدا، كما ذكره. والقسم الآخر أن يكون ذلك المفهوم في تلك الكثرة لا على السواء، بل إما أن يكون في بعضها أقدم أو أولى أو أشد أو أكثر، وهو كالأبيض على الثلج والعاج، والموجود على الجوهر والعرض. وفي هذا القسم لا يجب أن تكون مقتضيات تلك المفهومات واحدة، بل ربّما تختلف، مثل اسم الضوء الواقع على ضوء الشمس وضوء القمر وضوء النار، وضوء الشمس يقتضي زوال العشيّ دون سائر الأضواء.

والوجود من هذا القبيل، فإنه يكون في الواجب قائما بذاته من غير عروضه لماهيته، وفي غير الواجب يكون عارضا لماهيته.
notes: READING NOTE  Two points are different: the common mental concept and the real existence to which it refers. Ṭūsī uses graded or analogical predication [التشكيك]; he does not say that the Necessary and the possible are merely homonyms.

extracts.title: Qūnawī: knowing the Real by the Real
extracts.english:
We say that sound spiritual tasting [الذوق الصحيح], which the people of the Real have been granted by Him, entails that their knowing begins with knowledge of the Real—but through the Real, not through their own faculties and intellects. Once they know the Real through the Real, they know themselves through Him, in the respect in which they have known Him; thereafter they know whatever the Real wills to disclose to them, all at once or by stages. For this reason, in our view no one can know the reality of anything without knowing the Real.

We indicated earlier, in the introduction, that the Real as determined in the conception of any intellectual knower—whether His existence is said to be additional to His reality or identical with it—cannot correspond to what the Real is in Himself, or to the determination He has for Himself insofar as He is distinguished from what is other than Him.

Consequently, neither the claim that the Real’s existence is identical with His reality nor the claim that existence is a necessary concomitant of His reality yields a genuine realization [تحقيق]. Neither account can be established completely.
extracts.arabic:
ونحن نقول: إنّ من مقتضى الذوق الصحيح الذي خطئ به أهل الحق منه سبحانه أنّ مبدأ معرفتهم معرفة الحق، لكن بالحق لا بقواهم وعقولهم. فإذا عرفوا الحق بالحق، عرفوا بعد ذلك نفوسهم بالحق من حيث ما عرفوه به، ثم عرفوا ما شاء الحق أن يطلعهم عليه دفعة أو بالتدريج. ولهذا يستحيل عندنا أن يعرف أحد حقيقة شيء، ما لم يعرف الحق.

وقد ذكرنا قبل هذا على سبيل التلويح في التمهيد أنّ تعيّن الحق — سواء قيل بأنّ وجوده زائد على حقيقته أو أنّ وجوده عين حقيقته — في تعقّل كل عاقل لا يمكن أن يكون مطابقا لما هو الحق عليه في نفسه ولا لتعيّنه عند نفسه من حيث ما يمتاز عن سواه.

فحينئذ سواء قول من يقول بأنّ وجود الحق عين حقيقته وقول من يقول بأنّ وجوده من لوازم حقيقته، لا يحصل من الأمرين تحقيق إذ لا يتمّ تقرير كل واحد من الأمرين.
notes: READING NOTE  The epistemic claim is stronger than mere limits on natural theology: Qūnawī proposes the priority of divinely given knowledge of the Real. The online Arabic reads «خطئ به», which is awkward and likely a transcription error for «خُصّ به»; the translation follows the contextual sense “granted” pending collation against Schubert’s print edition. This uncertainty is not evidence of a variant manuscript reading.

extracts.title: Ṭūsī’s unexpected response to the appeal to unveiling
extracts.english: Concerning his statement, “We say that sound spiritual tasting entails ...,” to the end of the section, I say: This discourse is of the utmost excellence and perfection. Someone who has no share of what God—glorified be He—bestows upon those who turn toward His presence by the path of unveiling [الكشف] cannot attain it. May God make us among His friends who reach that station, if He wills. He is the giver of success [التوفيق].
extracts.arabic: قوله: «ونحن نقول: إنّ من مقتضى الذوق الصحيح» إلى آخر الفصل. أقول: هذا كلام في غاية الحسن والكمال، لا يقف عليه من لا يكون له حظ مما يفيض اللّه سبحانه على المتوجهين إلى جنابه بطريق الكشف. جعلنا اللّه من أوليائه الواصلين إلى تلك المرتبة إن شاء، وهو ولي التوفيق.
notes: READING NOTE  This is Ṭūsī speaking, not Qūnawī. It is direct positive appraisal of this spiritual account; it must not be inflated into Ṭūsī’s abandonment of the philosophical arguments he has just defended.

extracts.title: Are possible quiddities themselves made?
extracts.english:
Second question. Are possible quiddities [الماهيات الممكنة] made [مجعولة], or are they not made? Whichever answer is given, are they—considered simply as quiddities—existential realities possessing some manner of existence, or are they nonexistential?

If they are unmade, they cannot be existential realities. For that would put them on the same footing as the Necessary in intrinsic necessity of existence [وجوب الوجود الذاتي] and in the sheer unity of essence. They would no longer be possible, but necessary, since they would lack the possibility and poverty entailed by receiving existence from another.
extracts.arabic:
المسألة الثانية: هل الماهيات الممكنة مجعولة أو غير مجعولة؟ وعلى كلا التقديرين، فهل هي من كونها ماهيات فقط أمور وجودية بمعنى أنّ لها ضربا من الوجود أو هي أمور عدمية؟

إن كانت غير مجعولة، فلا جائز أن تكون وجودية، لأنه يلزم من ذلك مساوقتها للواجب في وجوب الوجود الذاتي وفي صرافة الوحدة الذاتية، ولم تكن حينئذ ممكنة، بل واجبة لخلوّها عن وصف الإمكان والفقر المستلزم لاستفادة الوجود من الغير.
notes: READING NOTE  The question is not simply whether the objects of divine knowledge are “real.” It asks what is produced by the act of making: quiddity itself, its existence, or its determination. The remaining horns of Qūnawī’s lengthy dilemma are not included here.
Arabic source: https://www.ibnalarabi.com/qunawi/tusi.php?id=3

extracts.title: Ṭūsī: quiddity by itself and its intellectual and extramental existence
extracts.english:
Rather, the truth is that all quiddities and existents are made: God—glorified and exalted—is their maker. When we say that possible quiddities are related to existence, possibility [الإمكان] is not attributable to quiddity precisely insofar as it is quiddity alone. It can be attributed when quiddity is compared with existence or nonexistence.

As for the question, “Are quiddities, simply as quiddities, existential realities?” the answer is no. Quiddity, precisely insofar as it is quiddity, can be nothing other than quiddity.

But if the question means, “Do they have some manner of existence?” the answer is yes. When a quiddity is conceived, it acquires intellectual existence [وجود عقلي]; when it is posited among extramental individuals, it has extramental existence [وجود عيني]. Extramental existence comes only from its producer; intellectual existence arises through whoever conceives it. Both modes of existence are possible for it.

When they say that a quiddity has an existence before itself, they mean the conception of it that causes its extramental existence: this is productive knowledge [العلم الفعلي]. When they say it has existence accompanying it, they mean extramental existence. When they say it has an existence after itself, they mean its being conceived after its extramental existence—receptive knowledge [العلم الانفعالي]. If quiddity alone is considered, nothing is intended by the intellect except quiddity itself; neither existence nor nonexistence enters into that consideration. Hence it is said that quiddity is neither existent nor nonexistent.
extracts.arabic:
بل الحقّ أنّ جميع الماهيات والموجودات مجعولة، جاعلها اللّه سبحانه وتعالى. وإذا قلنا: الماهيات الممكنة صارت منسوبة إلى الوجود، فإنّ الإمكان لا يمكن أن توصف به الماهية من حيث هي ماهية فقط، إنما يمكن أن توصف به إذا قيست إلى الوجود أو إلى العدم.

وأما قوله: «هل هي من كونها ماهيات فقط أمور وجودية؟». فالجواب: لا، فإنّ الماهية من حيث هي ماهية فقط لا يمكن أن تكون شيئا غير الماهية.

وأما إذا فسّره بقوله: «هل لها ضرب من الوجود؟». فالجواب: نعم، فإنّ الماهية إذا تصوّرت، حدث لها وجود عقلي. وإذا فرضت في الأعيان، كان لها وجود عيني. والوجود العيني لا يكون إلّا من موجدها، والوجود العقلي يكون ممن تعقّلها. وكلا الوجودين ممكن له. وإذا قالوا: للماهية وجود قبلها، أرادوا به تعقّلها الذي يكون سببا لوجودها العيني. وهو العلم الفعلي. وإذا قالوا: لها وجود معها، أرادوا به الوجود العيني. وإذا قالوا: لها وجود بعدها، أرادوا به تعقّلها بعد وجودها، يعني العلم الانفعالي. وإذا نظر إلى الماهية فقط، لم يكن في القصد العقلي إلا الماهية، ولم يكن الوجود ولا العدم داخلين في ذلك النظر. ولذلك قالوا: إنها ليست بموجودة ولا معدومة.
notes: READING NOTE  The final denial is made in the restricted consideration of quiddity in itself. It should not be read as granting independently existing nonexistent objects. The source ends this selected passage before Ṭūsī’s next qualification concerning the quiddity actually obtaining in a mind.

extracts.title: Ṭūsī: common existence exists as a universal only in intellect
extracts.english:
Common universal existence [الوجود العام المشترك] obtains only in the intellect; the same applies to every common universal. An extramental individual thing cannot be predicated of several things. If it were in each one, it would not be numerically the same thing but many things. If it were in the whole precisely as a whole, the whole in that respect would be one thing, and it would not be predicated of many. If it were in the whole in the sense of being distributed among its individuals, each individual would have only a part of it, not that very thing. And if it were in neither the individuals nor the whole, it would be predicated of neither.

In sum, for something to apply to another is for it to be predicated of that other; predication and the assignment of a subject belong only to the intellect. Hence common universal existence can only be intellectual. As such, its obtaining in the intellect depends on an intellect and is possible; it has another existence through which it is established [ثابت] in the intellect.
extracts.arabic: الوجود العام المشترك لا يتحقق إلا في العقل، وكذلك في كل أمر عام مشترك. وذلك أنّ الشيء العيني لا يقع على أشياء متعددة. فإنه إن كان في كل واحد من تلك الأشياء، لم يكن شيئا بعينه، بل كان أشياء. وإن كان في الكلّ من حيث هو كلّ، والكلّ من تلك الحيثية شيء واحد، فلم يقع على أشياء. وإن كان في الكلّ بمعنى التفرّق في آحاده، كان في كل واحد جزء من ذلك الشيء، لا نفس ذلك الشيء. وإن لم يكن في شيء من الآحاد، ولا في الكل، لم يكن واقعا عليها. وبالجملة، وقوعه على غيره لا يكون إلا حمله على ذلك الغير. والحمل والوضع لا يكون إلا في العقل. والوجود العامّ المشترك لا يمكن أن يكون إلا عقليّا. وإذا كان كذلك، كان حصوله في العقل بسبب العقل، وكان ممكنا. ويكون له وجود آخر هو بذلك الوجود يكون ثابتا في العقل.
notes: READING NOTE  Crucial distinction: Ṭūsī is not denying extramental existents. He denies that one numerical extramental existence is a universal literally distributed through many individuals. This challenges any simple identification of “the common concept of existence” with a single extramental existent.
